title: Tensor decomposition at Kruskal’s uniqueness threshold
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized algorithm that, for every real third-order tensor having a decomposition satisfying Kruskal’s condition, recovers its rank decomposition in polynomial time in the exact algebraic model specified below? More precisely, are there constants \(C,c>0\) and one finite program whose cost is at most \(C(N+1)^c\) on every run and whose probability of outputting a correct decomposition is at least \(2/3\) on every promised input, where \(N=n_1n_2n_3\) is the number of input entries? The number of components and all Kruskal ranks may grow with the dimensions and are not supplied to the program.

source_formulation.text: Is there an algorithm for decomposing T under the conditions of Kruskal’s uniqueness theorem?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

why: Kruskal’s condition guarantees that latent factors are mathematically determined by their tensor, but uniqueness alone does not provide an efficient recovery algorithm. Polynomial-time recovery throughout that regime connects identifiability with computation in models used for learning and signal analysis.
status_note: Resolved for the explicitly stated exact real algebraic model by Sivan, arXiv:2609.13693v1, posted 12 September 2026, Theorem 2.1. The full proof and the implication from Kruskal’s promise were checked on 2026-09-16. The source is a preprint; the result is not represented as a verified Lean formalization or as a solution of bit-complexity or noisy-recovery variants.

sentences: A third-order tensor is represented as a sum of outer products of three families of vectors.
Kruskal’s condition guarantees uniqueness when the three Kruskal ranks sum to at least twice the number of components plus two.
The historical question asks for polynomial-time recovery throughout that entire regime, with the number of components allowed to grow.
A September 2026 preprint gives such recovery in an exact real algebraic model that permits univariate root finding.
After checking its proof and scope, this exact-recovery card is archived as resolved, while the separate questions about noisy data and finite-precision computation are not claimed solved.

context_blocks.text: The source asks about algorithms throughout Kruskal’s uniqueness regime and separately discusses robustness to noisy entries. This card selects the exact polynomial-time recovery question. The explicit real algebraic model, including univariate root finding, follows the model of the 2026 resolution and states the output convention that the original short question leaves implicit. It does not assert a solution of the separate robust or bit-complexity questions.

In ICALP 2026, Bhargava, Schulman and Sivan proved a randomized \((n_1+n_2+n_3)^{O(k)}\) upper bound, where \(k=2R+2-\max\{k_A+k_B,k_A+k_C,k_B+k_C\}\). This supplies an algorithmic proof and polynomial time for fixed \(k\), but its exponent need not be constant throughout the full uniqueness regime.

Sivan’s September 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time recovery under the more general Lovitz–Petrov condition. Its Theorem 2.1 applies, in particular, to every Kruskal-promised tensor. The result uses exact real algebraic computation with polynomial-time univariate root finding, explicitly stated in footnote 2.

The September result is a preprint, not a claim of an already checked Lean proof. The theorem, full correctness argument, Kruskal-to-Lovitz–Petrov implication and model transfer were read during this review. Its probability-one generic choices fit the continuous-randomness model fixed here.

definitions:
An input consists of positive integers \(n_1,n_2,n_3\) in binary and the explicitly listed real entries of an array \(T\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_2\times n_3}\), held in exact real registers. It is promised that, for some integer \(R\ge2\), there exist nonzero vectors \(a_j\in\mathbb R^{n_1}\), \(b_j\in\mathbb R^{n_2}\), \(c_j\in\mathbb R^{n_3}\), \(1\le j\le R\), such that \(T_{uvw}=\sum_{j=1}^{R}(a_j)_u(b_j)_v(c_j)_w\). Write \(A=[a_1|\cdots|a_R]\), and likewise \(B,C\). The Kruskal rank \(k_A\) is the largest integer \(k\in\{0,\ldots,R\}\) for which every choice of \(k\) distinct columns of \(A\) is linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\); the empty choice is independent. The promise is \(k_A+k_B+k_C\ge2R+2\). No hidden vectors, rank values, decomposition certificate, conditioning bound or generic-position assumption beyond this promise are provided.

Tensor rank is the minimum number of nonzero rank-one terms in any such sum over \(\mathbb R\). Kruskal’s theorem states that the promised \(R\) is the tensor rank and that its decomposition is unique up to reordering and componentwise nonzero rescaling. A valid output is \(R\) and three explicitly listed real factor matrices giving exactly \(T\). Permuting their columns together, or multiplying the three columns of component \(j\) by nonzero scalars whose product is \(1\), gives an equivalent output. Exact equality of all tensor entries is required; an approximation or a decomposition with more terms is not the specified output.

The computational model is an exact algebraic random-access machine with real registers and finite binary control. Copying, reading or writing a real register, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and comparison of two reals each cost one operation. The only built-in real constants are \(0\) and \(1\). Integer arithmetic and control use ordinary binary bit operations, which also count. The model additionally has a real-root operation: given an explicitly listed coefficient vector \((u_0,\ldots,u_m)\) of a nonzero univariate polynomial, it returns all distinct real roots in increasing order, at cost \(m+1\); the coefficient-list construction and output storage count separately. This degree-cost convention is equivalent for polynomial-time existence to charging any fixed polynomial in the degree. An identically zero polynomial, or a division by zero, must be detected and handled without an undefined operation.

Each random instruction draws one independent real uniformly from \([0,1]\), at unit cost. Probability is taken over the product of these draws; the total running-time bound must hold on every run, including exceptional draws, on which the program may return failure. The finite program is independent of dimensions and input entries and has no advice, arbitrary input-dependent constants, multivariate-system oracle, floor operation or transcendental primitive. All reads, output writes, root calls and integer work are charged. The guarantee is a worst-case input bound with bounded failure probability, not an average over input tensors. This is an algebraic operation bound: it does not assert a bit-complexity or numerical-conditioning guarantee for approximations to the real entries.
answer_criterion: The historical benchmark asks for a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm with the stated polynomial cost and success guarantee for every promised tensor, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists in this precise model. A bound whose exponent depends on \(R\) or on a Kruskal rank does not establish a uniform polynomial bound. This record is archived after checking an affirmative algebraic-model result; the editorial verification does not itself supply a Lean formalization.

checked_sources: Read all three pages of the 2014 primary source, including Definition 2, Theorem 3, Open Problem 4 and the separate robust question.

Read ICALP 2026 Theorem 1, its parameter definition and explicit statement that general polynomial-time efficiency remains unsettled, plus the exact-real model and root-finding subroutines in Sections 3–4.

Read all of Sivan arXiv:2609.13693v1 pages 1–12, including Theorem 2.1, Lemma 2.2, Rado-based Corollaries 2.4–2.5 and Claim 2.6; confirmed arXiv submission 12 September and internal manuscript date 10 September 2026.

Independently checked the Kruskal-to-LP transfer: for a size-s subset, each factor submatrix has rank at least min(k_i,s); the concave function sum_i min(k_i,s)-2s has value at least 2 at endpoints s=2 and s=R. The Kruskal condition forces each k_i>=2. Hence all 2<=s<=R satisfy LP.

Checked the proof chain: Rado gives generic independent two-planes with simultaneous pair-extension ranks; the skew-symmetric contractions have their direct-sum image; a second generic covector separates the quotient lines; the stated spectral projectors isolate individual rank-two summands. A generically nonzero off-diagonal block recovers two factor directions, and the full-column-rank Khatri–Rao product determines the third factors.

Checked compression and restoration: mode flattenings reveal the factor spans under the Kruskal promise because the two-mode Khatri–Rao factors have full column rank. These changes of basis preserve all column-dependence relations and have polynomial algebraic cost; tensor rank and factor matrices need not be supplied.

Model transfer: uniform draws in [0,1] have densities, so the finitely many proper algebraic bad sets and proper conditional hyperplanes have probability zero. Sample the second covector in a computed kernel basis. Polynomially many finite operations, including explicit-degree roots and square roots, suffice. Exceptional dimensions, noninvertibility and invalid blocks can be guarded and return failure within the same polynomial budget. This verifies the weaker success probability 2/3 without claiming a finite-bit-randomness or conditioning theorem.
This is editorial verification of a fresh preprint, not peer-review status or Lean proof verification. No conclusion about the separate robust/noisy task is drawn.
